raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused predominantly by immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL) or transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), the latter occurring as wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt) or variant ATTR (ATTRv) due to pathogenic TTR variants [1-4]. These entities share extracellular myocardial amyloid deposition but differ fundamentally in biology, tempo, prognosis, and treatment: AL reflects a plasma-cell dyscrasia with direct light-chain cardiotoxicity and requires urgent hematologic therapy, whereas ATTR reflects TTR tetramer destabilization, misfolding, and progressive myocardial infiltration [3,4]. Contemporary cohorts have reframed cardiac amyloidosis from a rare autopsy diagnosis to an important cause of heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, particularly in older men, Black patients with Val122Ile/Val142Ile ATTRv, and patients with aortic stenosis or musculoskeletal “red flags” [5-9].

Clinical suspicion remains the key diagnostic step. Typical presentations include exertional dyspnea, edema, orthostatic intolerance, atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, discordance between increased left ventricular wall thickness and low electrocardiographic voltage, intolerance of vasodilators, nephrotic-range proteinuria, peripheral/autonomic neuropathy, biceps tendon rupture, lumbar spinal stenosis, and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome [1,2,26,27]. Echocardiography commonly shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, reduced tissue Doppler velocities, impaired longitudinal function, and relative apical sparing of longitudinal strain, a useful but imperfect clue rather than a standalone diagnostic test [10]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization; diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and abnormal gadolinium kinetics suggest amyloid infiltration, while native T1 and extracellular volume quantify burden and may identify earlier disease [11,12].

The diagnostic algorithm should first exclude AL amyloidosis with serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation, because AL is a medical emergency and bone scintigraphy alone cannot safely distinguish all cases [1,2,4]. If monoclonal testing is negative, grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake on technetium-labeled bone-avid scintigraphy with appropriate SPECT imaging is highly specific for ATTR cardiac amyloidosis and can avoid endomyocardial biopsy [13,14]. If monoclonal studies are positive, if scintigraphy is equivocal, or if atypical features exist, tissue confirmation with amyloid typing—preferably by mass spectrometry—is essential [1,2]. Once ATTR is diagnosed, TTR genetic testing is mandatory to distinguish ATTRwt from ATTRv and to enable family counseling [1,2].

Risk stratification is biomarker-centered but should be individualized. In AL amyloidosis, cardiac troponin, NT-proBNP, and the involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference underpin staging, while NT-proBNP response after therapy is a validated surrogate for outcome [15,17]. In ATTR, NT-proBNP, renal function, troponin, functional class, 6-minute walk distance, and imaging burden inform prognosis; National Amyloidosis Centre staging using NT-proBNP and estimated glomerular filtration rate is widely applied [16]. Across subtypes, atrial mechanical dysfunction and intracardiac thrombus risk may be disproportionate, so anticoagulation is generally favored for atrial fibrillation irrespective of conventional CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimates [1,2].

Management combines supportive heart-failure care, rhythm management, and disease-modifying therapy. Loop diuretics are the cornerstone for congestion, often with cautious mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist use; beta-blockers, angiotensin inhibitors, and vasodilators are frequently poorly tolerated because stroke volume is fixed and autonomic dysfunction is common [1,2]. Pacemakers treat symptomatic conduction disease, but implantable defibrillator benefit is uncertain because electromechanical dissociation is a frequent terminal rhythm [1,2]. Selected patients may undergo valve intervention, transplantation, or combined organ strategies in expert centers.

AL cardiac amyloidosis requires rapid suppression of the amyloidogenic clone. Bortezomib-based cyclophosphamide–bortezomib–dexamethasone established high clonal response rates, and daratumumab added to this backbone has become a major first-line advance, improving hematologic complete response and organ responses in newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis [18,19]. Autologous stem-cell transplantation remains appropriate for carefully selected low-risk patients, but advanced cardiac involvement demands modified regimens and multidisciplinary oversight [1,4].

ATTR therapy has expanded rapidly. Tafamidis, a TTR stabilizer, reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in ATTR-CM and showed durable survival benefit with earlier continuous treatment [20,21]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer, improved a hierarchical composite outcome in ATTR-CM [22]. Gene-silencing therapies reduce hepatic TTR production: patisiran improved functional and quality-of-life measures in ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, while vutrisiran reduced all-cause death and recurrent cardiovascular events in HELIOS-B [23,24]. Earlier neuropathy trials of patisiran and inotersen established the RNA-targeting principle in hereditary ATTR, and tafamidis was first validated in familial amyloid polyneuropathy [28-30]. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing has shown proof-of-concept TTR knockdown, but long-term safety and cardiac outcomes remain under study [25]. The central challenge is now implementation: earlier recognition, precise amyloid typing, equitable access to genetic testing and costly disease-modifying therapies, and longitudinal assessment of whether combination or sequence strategies can halt or reverse myocardial amyloid burden.
